opening.argument: The report begins with a customer whose gift card had a zero balance when he tried to use it, then describes someone else using the card at a Dallas restaurant. The Dallas location said the card number and PIN had been keyed in. These are reported signs of gift-card draining, not a pitch to viewers. The discussion of software and keyboard activity explains the alleged mechanism; it does not ask the audience to use it. The report also examines whether card numbers and PINs are concealed and relays a retailer statement about reimbursement. That consumer-protection context matters: the segment investigates a reported problem and the response to it, without establishing any broader losses or outcomes.

citations.quote: But when he tried to use it at this restaurant in California, the manager said the card had a zero balance.
Someone else was already using it at an Outback in Dallas to buy drinks and appetizers.
The Dallas location told us the customer had the card number and PIN and both had been keyed in,.
Attorneys with the Federal Trade Commission say this is called gift card draining. We searched several stores and found while some cards hide the numbers and pins, others are easy to see.
However, older cards may still be found on shelves. Of course, if this happens, we fully reimburse our customers.
